title: New Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Everything you need to know
content:
Macworld






New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance
What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional connectivity. 
Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026
Price: From $2,499/£2,499
Pre-orders: Pre-order now
On sale: Shipping starts on September 22, 2026  but the Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October.
Apple has launched a new Mac Studio to replace the M4 Max and M3 Ultra model introduced 17 months ago, in March 2025. Externally, the 2026 Mac Studio retains what Apple calls its “signature compact design,” with the most significant upgrades taking place inside.
The previous generation was unusual because it mixed chip generations, pairing M4 Max with M3 Ultra. The 2026 models bring both tiers into the M5 family, with M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU, while M5 Ultra scales to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Neural Accelerators are now built into every GPU core to boost AI performance.
Apple claims up to 1.3x faster CPU performance, 1.8x faster graphics and 4.3x faster AI performance, depending on the configuration and workload. M5 Max also adds third-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing, while M5 Ultra can play up to 33 streams of 8K ProRes 422 video simultaneously. Elsewhere, PCIe Gen 6-based SSDs deliver up to twice the storage performance, while Apple’s N1 chip adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. USB-C genlock, support for up to eight displays, and Thunderbolt 5 clustering for distributed AI workloads are also new.


When is the new Mac Studio available?
The new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra was announced on August 25, 2026, but it won’t start shipping until September 22. Even then, not every configuration will be available: Apple says Mac Studio models configured with 512GB of unified memory won’t arrive until “late October.”
You can pre-order the new Mac Studio now, though, and if you want one we’d recommend ordering early. Ongoing chip and component shortages have constrained Mac availability, so the most popular configurations could quickly become difficult to find.
Pre-order the Mac Studio at Apple
Pre-order the Mac Studio at Apple U.K.


							




How much does the new Mac Studio cost?


ModelPrice
M5 Max, 36GB, 512GB$2,499 / $2,499 
M5 Ultra, 96GB, 1TB$5,499 / $5,499 

 



Has the Mac Studio price gone up?
In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Studio by $500, from $1,999 to $2,499. The M3 Ultra model saw an even steeper increase, rising $1,300 from its $3,999 launch price to $5,299. The hikes were part of broader increases across the Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to sharply higher component costs, particularly RAM.
The new M5 Max Mac Studio remains at the June price of $2,499, but the M5 Ultra model has risen by another $200 to $5,499. That makes it $1,500 more expensive than the previous-generation Ultra model was when it launched in March 2025.
Here’s a breakdown of the key price changes for the Mac Studio:


ModelOriginal PriceJune Price Update price
M4 Max, 36GB, 512GB$1,999 / £2,099$2,499 / £2,499$2,499 / $2,499 
M3 Ultra, 96GB, 1TB$3,999 / £4,199 $5,299 / £5,299$5,499 / $5,499 

 



When it comes to high prices, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio is filling the gap left by the the removal of the Mac Pro from the line up back in March 2026. 


Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra specs

				
					

				
			
Petter Ahrnstedt




Mac Studio moves to M5 Max and M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 512GB unified memory and 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth. Storage now uses PCIe Gen 6 for twice the performance, while connectivity adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and USB-C genlock. 
Processor: M5 Ultra and M5 Max chip compared
The Mac Studio comes with either Apple’s Max or Ultra chips. The Max chip is aimed at demanding professional and creative workflows and supports large amounts of unified memory and high memory bandwidth. The Max chip is also available as an option for the MacBook Pro. 
The Ultra chip combines two Max chips on one large chip using Apple’s UltraFusion architecture, so they offer double the CPU and GPU resources, and even higher memory capacity and bandwidth. It’s suited to complex 3D rendering, large AI models and scientific computing. 
M5 Max: We are already familiar with the M5 Max from the MacBook Pro that launched in March 2026. It offers an 18-core CPU and up to 40-core GPU, versus up to 16 CPU cores in the M4 Max. Its GPU includes a Neural Accelerator in every core, helping deliver up to 3.9x faster AI performance than M4 Max, according to Apple, alongside third-generation ray tracing. 
M5 Ultra: The M5 Ultra is a brand new chip that combines two M5 Max dies and offers up to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Apple claims up to 1.3x faster CPU, 1.8x faster graphics and 4.3x AI compute versus M3 Ultra.


						

							


Storage 
Maximum storage remains 16TB, so capacity hasn’t increased. 
The storage should be much faster though. Apple has introduced a next-generation SSD architecture based on PCIe Gen 6, which it claims delivers up to twice the storage performance. That should mean faster project loading, file transfers and loading of very large local AI models


						

							


RAM
Maximum unified memory remains 128GB with M5 Max and 512GB with M5 Ultra, the same as the previous generation. 
Bandwidth has improved though. The M5 Max will now reach 614GB/s, while M5 Ultra delivers 1.2TB/s. Apple says this represents a 50 percent increase in memory bandwidth over the previous generation.


						

							


Connectivity: WiFi & Bluetooth

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




Wi-Fi: The Mac Studio now supports Wi-Fi 7 which replaces the previous wireless standard Wi-Fi 6E.
Bluetooth: Bluetooth 6 replaces Bluetooth 5.3.
Ethernet: Existing connectivity including 10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, USB-A, SDXC and a headphone jack remains.




Thunderbolt: Thunderbolt 5 remains, offering up to 120Gb/s and as many as six Thunderbolt 5 ports depending on configuration. Thunderbolt 5 can now be used with RDMA to cluster multiple Mac Studios for distributed AI workloads; Apple says four systems can deliver up to 3x faster AI inference than one. 
Genlock: Apple has added Genlock support over USB-C. This is used for synchronising a display and camera (which can be an iPhone 17 Pro) and will be useful for professional video workflows.
Display support: The Mac Studio will support up to eight displays, including up to four Studio Display XDR displays at 5K/120Hz.
Other ports include two USB-C ports and an SDXD card slot on the front of the M5 Max model, and two Thunderbolt 5 ports and an SDXD card slot on the front of the M5 Max model. On the back of the Mac Studio are: 
4× Thunderbolt 5 ports
2× USB-A ports
1× HDMI port
1× 10Gb Ethernet port
1× 3.5mm headphone jack


						

							




Mac Studio M5 Max vs M4 Max: What’s Changed 


WhatWasNow

CPU14-core to 16-core M4 Max18-core M5 Max
GPU32-core to 40-core M4 Max32-core to 40-core M5 Max
Neural Accelerators16‑core Neural EngineDual 16‑core Neural Engine
Bandwidth546GB/s memory bandwidth614GB/s memory bandwidth
Max RAM96GB128GB

 



Mac Studio M5 Ultra vs M3 Ultra: What’s Changed 


WhatWasNow

CPU28-core to 32-core M3 Ultra30-core to 36-core M5 Ultra
GPU60-core to 80 core M3 Ultra64-core to 80-core M5 Ultra
Neural Accelerators32-core Neural Engine32-core Neural Engine
Bandwidth819GB/s memory bandwidth1.2TB/s memory bandwidth
Max RAM96GB512GB

 






Who is the Mac Studio best for?
Apple has designed the Mac Studio with M5 Max to meet the needs of demanding creative and technical professionals. Apple specifically highlights musicians, photographers, software developers, designers and 3D professionals. It’s also well suited to video editing, code compilation, AI image generation and running sizeable LLMs locally.
The Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is intended for professionals with exceptionally demanding workloads: VFX artists rendering complex scenes, filmmakers working with multiple streams of 8K video, engineers running simulations, and AI researchers or data scientists training and running huge models locally. Its 512GB memory ceiling is particularly valuable for frontier-class LLMs.


						

							


Should you buy the 2026 Mac Studio?
Availability is likely to be limited due to the global RAM shortages so we expect that stock will quickly run out.

title: Apple Magic Keyboards get cosmetic updates, avoid price hikes
content:
Macworld





If you’re planning on investing in a new M6 Mac mini or M5 Ultra Mac Studio, you might be buying a new Apple Magic Keyboard along with it. Apple has updated its keyboards, too: Certain keys have had their labels changed to symbols instead of names.
Apple introduced these changes with the MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air, so the company is basically catching up on normalizing the keys. The Tab, Caps Lock, Shift, Delete, and Return keys no longer have their respective word labels. Instead, they have arrow icons:
Tab is now ⇥
Caps Lock is now ⇪
Shift is now ⇧
Delete is now ⌫
Return looks similar to ↵ (see photo above)
The switch to the graphical labeling is an effort to standardize its keyboards. Apple’s non-English keyboards used symbols, and implementing them in the English keyboard streamlines the production process. However, Apple did not update the keys on the $129 wireless Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad that has a Lightning connection for charging.
Speaking of the production process, it appears that the Magic Keyboards have not been affected by the worldwide RAM shortage (/sarcasm), so their prices have not changed:
USB-C Magic Keyboard: $99/£99
USB-C Magic Keyboard with Touch ID: $149/£149
USB-C Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad: $179/£179 (white); $199/£199 (black)

title: New Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro: Everything you need to know
content:
Macworld






New Mac mini 2026: At a glance
What’s new: The 2026 Mac mini delivers much faster performance, especially for graphics and AI, thanks to the M6 and M5 Pro chips. It also brings faster storage and upgraded connectivity, with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard.
Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026
Price: From $899/£899
Pre-orders: Pre-order now
On sale: September 22, 2026
Apple has launched a new Mac mini to replace the M4 and M4 Pro Mac mini which was introduced in October 2024. Externally the 2026 Mac mini looks just as it did following the redesign in October 2024 – it’s still a five-by-five-inch square with two front USB-C ports and the headphone jack, with three Thunderbolt ports, HDMI and Ethernet on the rear. It’s what’s inside that has changed.
The new Mac mini models offer new chips, the M6 and the M5 Pro. This is a similar scenario to a few years ago when Apple launched the M4 Mac Studio alongside the M3 Ultra Mac Studio. There is likely to be some confusion about the chip generations so we will explain the differences in more detail below.
These new chips will offer a significant jump in performance, especially relating to AI. With this update it is particularly apparent that Apple is positioning the Mac mini as an AI machine.


When is the new Mac mini available?
The new Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro models were announced on August 25, 2026, but they won’t actually ship until September 22.
You can pre-order now though, and if you want one we recommend doing so because the chip shortages that have plagued the industry are likely to mean stock quickly runs out.
Pre-order the Mac mini at Apple
Pre-order the Mac mini at Apple U.K.

ModelPrice
M6, 16GB, 256GB$899 / $899 
M6, 16GB, 512GB$1,199 / $1,199 
M5 Pro, 24GB, 512GB$1,699 / $1,699

 



Has the Mac mini price gone up?
In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac mini by $200, from $599 to $799. The increase was part of a broader price hike across the entire Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to an unprecedented rise in component costs, particularly RAM.
We had hoped this meant Mac mini pricing would remain at the June level for the foreseeable future. Unfortunately, with the arrival of the new models, Apple has raised prices again—this time by a further $100/£100.
Here’s a breakdown of the key price changes for the Mac mini:


ChipOriginal PriceJune Price Update price
M4, 16GB, 256GB$599 / £599 $799 / £799 $899 / $899 
M4, 16GB, 512GB$799 / £799 $999 / £999 $1,199 / $1,199 
M5 Pro, 24GB, 512GB$1,399 / £1,399 $1,599 / £1,599 $1,699 / $1,699

 



This is no longer a budget Mac.


Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro specs
As well as the move from M4 and M4 Pro to M6 and M5 Pro, the Mac mini also gains storage that is up to twice as fast, according to Apple, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, 2.5Gb Ethernet and USB-C genlock support. 

				
					

				
			
The new M6 chip has launched in the Mac mini. 

Apple




Processor: M6 and M5 Pro chip compared
There may be some confusion over the chip generations in the new Mac mini. The mainstream model uses the newer M6 chip, while the more powerful model uses the older-generation M5 Pro. Pro chips are designed for heavier professional workloads, with more CPU and GPU cores, higher memory bandwidth, support for more unified memory, additional displays and faster Thunderbolt connectivity. So while M5 Pro remains the more capable chip overall, M6 offers a significant step up from the standard M5 and an even larger jump from the M4 in the previous generation Mac mini.
M6: The Mac mini is the first Mac to ship with the M6 chip, replacing the M4 in the entry-level model. It features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from 10 CPU and GPU cores in the previous generation, and supports up to 32GB of unified memory with 170GB/s memory bandwidth. Apple promises up to 40% faster CPU performance, twice the graphics performance and up to 4x faster AI performance than M4. It also introduces Apple’s first Dual 16-core Neural Engine, delivering up to twice the Neural Engine performance.
M5 Pro: The M5 Pro replaces the M4 Pro in the higher-end Mac mini and can be configured with up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU. Apple claims up to 4x faster LLM processing, 1.4x faster Blender ray-tracing performance and 1.5x faster Affinity image processing than M4 Pro. It supports up to 64GB of unified memory with 307GB/s memory bandwidth. Both chips feature Neural Accelerators in their GPU cores, but the M5 Pro’s additional CPU and GPU cores, greater memory capacity and higher bandwidth make it better suited to video production, 3D rendering, development and larger local AI models.
With both of these chips the focus is very much on AI with Apple emphasising that both the M6 and M5 Pro incorporate Neural Accelerators in their GPU cores. 


						

							


Storage 
Apple claims the new Mac mini offers up to 2x faster storage compared to the previous generation. 
Other than that the storage capacities are as before – 256GB,  512GB, 1TB and 2TB for the M6 model and 512GB, 1TB, 2TB, 4TB and 8TB SSDs for the M5 Pro model. 


						

							


RAM
The new M6 model supports 32GB RAM unlike the M4 model which maxed out at 24GB. 
The new M5 Pro model supports a maximum of 654GB RAM, up from 48GB. 


						

							


Connectivity: WiFi & Bluetooth

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary / Foundry




Wi-Fi: Both models now support Wi-Fi 7 which replaces the previous wireless standard Wi-Fi 6E.
Bluetooth: Both models also move to Bluetooth 6, replacing Bluetooth 5.3.
Ethernet: Previously faster Ethernet was an upgrade; the new models now have 2.5Gb Ethernet, with 10Gb Ethernet available as a configurable option.
Thunderbolt: The M6 Mac mini has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and the the M5 Pro version has three Thunderbolt 5 ports. This is the same as the previous generation.
Genlock: Apple has added Genlock support over USB-C. This is used for synchronising a display and camera (which can be an iPhone 17 Pro). It is aimed at professional video workflows
Display support: The M6 Mac mini will support up to two 6K displays plus one 5K display, while the M5 Pro supports up to three 6K displays. 
Other ports include two USB-C/USB 3 ports and a headphone jack on the front and HDMI and Ethernet remain on the rear, as previously.

Who is the Mac mini best for?
The M6 Mac mini will suit someone who wants a fast, compact desktop Mac.
The M5 Pro Mac mini is aimed at developers and creative or technical professionals who need more CPU and GPU performance, memory or Thunderbolt bandwidth, but don’t require the greater performance and expandability of a Mac Studio. It is particularly well suited to running AI models and agentic AI workloads locally.

Availability is likely to be limited due to the global RAM shortages so we expect that stock will quickly run out.

title: Amid raging price hikes, Apple slashes flagship cloth by more than 50%
content:
Macworld





On a day of high-priced product announcements, Apple has offered a crumb of comfort to its more cash-strapped customers: the beloved Polishing Cloth has dropped in price by a whopping 53 percent. Relentlessly memed on for charging a faintly absurd $19 for the square cloth at launch three years ago, the company is now happy to accept just $9 for seemingly the same product.
The common thread uniting Tuesday’s two big Mac updates was prices going up. The M6 Mac mini starts at $899, up from $599 for the equivalent M4 model just two months ago. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, starts at $5,499, a price hike of another $200 over the previous price hike. But the Polishing Cloth went against the grain with a huge price drop.
Apple didn’t send out a press release advertising the nonabrasive fabric accessory’s new bargain price. Instead, it quietly removed the previous store entry (which carried the product code MW693AM/A) and put up a new one in its place (MLH74AM/A) with an updated price. Other than the price and code, it appears to be an identical product with an identical description.
As before, that includes the endlessly amusing Compatibility section, which lists every iPhone and iPad going back to 2012, every single Apple Watch, and a huge list of MacBooks. In some ways, it’s surprising the company bothered to make the list since the description makes it clear that the Polishing Cloth cleans any Apple display, but we appreciate the effort.
Whether this bargain price will last remains to be seen. Unlike other Apple devices the Polishing Cloth is unlikely to be affected by the ongoing memory shortage, but we’ll be monitoring international microfiber shipments with the greatest of interest.

title: Apple Smart Home Display Still Coming This Year

Apple remains on track to launch its first smart home device with a screen before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Gurman reiterated that the device will use facial recognition to determine who is standing in front of it and serve up personalized content for that individual user. title: Solve tight spaces with this impossibly thin 45W wall charger (30% off)
content:
Macworld





		
Ugreen Nexode Air 45W
View Deal
Sometimes, when you move furniture around, there’s just no way around covering an outlet just enough that it makes it impossible to use with most chargers. Well, this super-slim Ugreen Nexode Air model is the perfect choice for such places, and it’s only going to cost you $27 now that it’s $13 off its MSRP. That’s a solid discount on a slim and fast little charger that can replace the bulky charging brick you carry around.
At only 0.57 inches thick, the Nexode Air has an ultra-slim, flat profile that can fit in tight spaces. Even better, it weighs next to nothing, and the prongs fold flat, so this charger can slip into a pocket without snagging. For commuting, travel, or business trips, it’s the perfect charger to pack up.
Don’t let the small size fool you, though. Thanks to GaN technology, this charger pushes out up to 45W of power. That’s enough to fast-charge your phone, taking an iPhone 17 from empty to 70 percent in just half an hour. That much power is also enough to handle tablets and even your MacBook Air. Instead of keeping a separate adapter for every gadget, you can grab this and know it’ll cover the whole range of devices.
One thing to keep in mind when buying this charger is that it features a single USB-C port, so it can only charge one device at a time. If you commonly need to power up multiple devices at once, you might want to look into a different model
At $27, an impressive 30 percent off its MSRP, the Ugreen Nexode Air 45W charger is a smart, affordable choice for anyone who wants fast charging in a pocket-friendly package.

content:
Macworld





While all eyes are on the upcoming iPhone event, Apple threw us a curveball Tuesday morning with a rare August launch of an updated Mac Studio with the all-new M5 Ultra processor.
The new Mac Studio is visually identical to the previous model but has major upgrades inside. Instead of the M4 Max and M3 Ultra, you can now buy a Mac Studio with an M5 Max or M5 Ultra processor, with up to a whopping 512GB of RAM. Here are the specs Apple is offering for the two chips:

While the M5 Ultra is still double the capability of the M5 Max, Apple touts its “next-generation UltraFusion technology to form a quad-die architecture for the first time in an M-series chip.” The previous UltraFusion interconnector linked two Max dies over 10,000 high-speed connections that offer low latency and high bandwidth. It was previously reported that Apple was working to create a new version of the Ultra chip with more advanced UltraFusion architecture.
Apple is leaning hard into AI and calls the M5 Ultra Mac Studio “a game changer for AI workloads” and says “AI coding agents process significantly faster, image generation tools can render creations in an instant, and enterprise teams can cluster multiple systems to scale performance to new heights.” 
In addition to the new chips, the Mac Studio now has an N1 chip to bring Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, as well as “a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.” We already praised the MacBook Pro for its super-fast storage speeds, and Apple now claims the new SSDs deliver “industry-leading read and write speeds for rapid project loading, file transfers, and loading huge LLMs.”
Now for the not-so-good news. While the M5 Max model starts at the same $2,499 as the post-price-hike M4 Max, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio now starts at $5,499, an increase of another $200 over the previous price hike. That means you’re paying $1,500 more than if you bought an M3 Ultra Mac Studio before June. You’re also paying more for storage and RAM, so get ready to shell out well over 20 grand for a fully loaded model (which won’t be available until October). The most expensive M5 Ultra you can get now, with 256GB of RAM and 16TB of storage, costs $18,299.
The M5 Mac Studio is available for pre-order now but won’t begin shipping until September 22.

title: Apple launches new M6 Mac mini with another price hike
content:
Macworld





As predicted on this site earlier today, Apple has announced the launch of a new Mac mini model with M5 and M6 chip options. It doesn’t feature any design changes or external upgrades, but it does offer a two-generation bump in processors compared to the previous model.
Slightly confusingly, the version of the Mac mini with a chip from the M5 generation is the more powerful of the two, because it’s the M5 Pro. This spec starts at $1,699 for a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, but customers have the option to bump that to 18 and 20 cores, respectively, for an additional $200. There are also configuration options to increase RAM from the starting 24GB or storage from the baseline 512GB, and to upgrade to 10 Gigabit Ethernet. The RAM options remain the same, but the 64GB highest-end option now costs $1,000.
More appealing for the Mac mini’s traditional budget market will be the M6 model, which starts at a far more manageable $899. That, however, is still a $100 increase over the M4 model from 2024 that it replaces. Worse, the M4 model started at just $599 until June, when Apple responded to the ongoing memory crunch by imposing brutal price hikes. In other words, the cheapest entry point to Apple’s desktop Mac ecosystem has jumped by $300, or 50 percent, in the space of two months.
The $899 version isn’t exactly a state-of-the-art build, either. The entry-level configuration comes with 16GB of RAM and just 256GB of storage. We should note that it is possible to get this spec for $799, but only if you’re an education buyer. Of note, the Mac mini is not available for the Apple Upgrade program either.

				
					

				
			
Apple




The price hike is likely to weaken the Mac mini’s appeal among budget buyers, but (aside from the necessity to accommodate increasing component costs) Apple may not care. In his report predicting that a new mini was on the way, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman noted that the machine had become increasingly popular for running AI applications locally, and that Apple was struggling to meet demand. The company may not mind if fewer customers are prepared to pay the asking price, since there are plenty of AI fans ready to take their place.
Those AI fans will likely be tempted by a new model with a new chip. Apple boasts that the M6 delivers “gains across every dimension of performance” and “the ideal balance of performance, power efficiency, and on-device AI to effortlessly fly through daily tasks, coding, and creative projects.”
In numerical terms, the company claims the M6 version of the Mac will deliver up to 4x faster AI performance, 2x faster storage and graphics, and 40% faster CPU performance than the M4 mini. The M5 Pro model, meanwhile, is rated by its maker as up to 8.5x faster at LLM prompt processing than its M2 Pro predecessor, and up to 4x faster than the M4 Pro model. Naturally we will put those claims to the test in our labs.
Another surprise is how early Apple has announced the new Mac mini. Pre-orders are open now, but it won’t go on sale until 22 September, almost a month from now.

title: Apple Unveils New Mac Studio With M5 Max and M5 Ultra Chips
content:
Apple today announced new Mac Studio models with the M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, the latter of which is the company's most powerful chip ever.


The new ‌Mac Studio‌ features a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6 that Apple says is up to twice as fast as before. The machine also gains Thunderbolt 5 ports with up to 120Gb/s of bandwidth, along with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 for the first time via Apple's N1 chip. The new ‌Mac Studio‌ also supports genlock over USB-C and can drive up to eight displays.

The M5 Ultra chip includes an up to 36-core CPU that contains 12 super cores and 24 performance cores. It delivers up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra from the previous generation ‌Mac Studio‌. 

M1 Ultra. Apple says the GPU's latest shader core technology, paired with second-generation Dynamic Caching, hardware-accelerated mesh shading, and third-generation ray tracing, delivers up to 40% faster graphics performance than the M3 Ultra. 

The chip also includes a more capable Media Engine, with dedicated hardware for H.264, HEVC, four ProRes encode and decode engines, and hardware-accelerated AV1 decode, along with a 32-core Neural Engine for on-device AI tasks.




The M5 Ultra is built by connecting two dual-die M5 Max chips using Apple's next-generation UltraFusion technology, which increases inter-die bandwidth to over 4.4TB/s and connection density by more than 6x, allowing the four dies to function as a single processor.

The new ‌Mac Studio‌ with the M5 Ultra supports up to 512GB of unified memory and up to 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, which is a 50% increase over M3 Ultra. Apple says the added memory and bandwidth allows users to store large datasets locally, increase tokens per second, and run large language models with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on device.

Users can also cluster multiple ‌Mac Studio‌ systems together using built-in support for Thunderbolt 5 and RDMA (remote direct memory access), creating a shared memory pool across systems. Apple says a cluster of four ‌Mac Studio‌ systems delivers up to 3x faster AI inference than a single system.

The ‌Mac Studio‌ is also now available with the M5 Max chip, offering an 18-core CPU with 6 super cores and 12 performance cores, up to 40 GPU cores, up to 128GB of unified memory with up to 614GB/s of memory bandwidth, and up to 8TB of storage. Apple says the M5 Max delivers up to 3.9x faster AI performance than the previous generation.

title: Apple Debuts M5 Ultra as Most Powerful Chip Ever
content:
Apple today announced the M5 Ultra, which the company says is its most powerful chip ever.


The M5 Ultra is built by connecting two dual-die M5 Max chips using Apple's next-generation UltraFusion technology, which is the first time Apple has used a quad-die architecture in an M-series chip. UltraFusion increases inter-die bandwidth to over 4.4TB/s and connection density by more than 6x, allowing the four dies to function as a single processor.

The chip includes an CPU with up to 36 cores, containing 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, delivering up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra.

Its GPU scales up to 80 cores, with a Neural Accelerator built into each core for the first time on an Ultra chip. Apple says this delivers up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance compared to the M3 Ultra, along with up to 1.8x faster graphics than the previous-generation chip.

The M5 Ultra also includes a 32-core Neural Engine and a more capable Media Engine, with twice the video encode and decode blocks as M5 Max, allowing users to simultaneously play up to 33 streams of 8K ProRes 422 at 30 fps.

The chip supports up to 512GB of unified memory and up to 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, a 50% increase over M3 Ultra. Apple says the added memory and bandwidth let users store large datasets locally, increase tokens per second, and run large language models with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on device.

The M6 chip is equipped with a 12-core CPU and a 12-core GPU, up from a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU in the M5 chip. In addition, the M6 chip features the first-ever dual Neural Engine with two 16-core engines, up from one in previous chips. Apple said the Mac mini with the M6 chip delivers up to 40% faster CPU performance, up to 4× faster performance for AI tasks in particular, up to 2× faster graphics performance, and up to 2× faster storage speeds compared to the previous-generation model with the 10-core M4 chip, 32GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage.

There are two M5 Pro configurations available, including one with a 15-core CPU and a 16-core GPU, and another with an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. Both of these models are equipped with a single 16-core Neural Engine for AI tasks.

For both the M6 and M5 Pro configurations, Apple said the Mac mini now includes Neural Accelerators in each GPU core for the first time. 

Apple silicon continues to deliver industry-leading performance-per-watt, and Apple said the M6 chip has the world's fastest CPU core. Apple touted the Mac mini as the "leading" desktop for "always-on, deskside agentic computing." 

press release provides many specific performance comparisons involving apps such as Affinity, Blender, LM Studio, and Photoshop.

All models still have two front USB-C ports, a front headphone jack, three rear Thunderbolt ports, a rear HDMI port, and a rear Ethernet port that is now a 2.5 Gigabit port by default, up from 1 Gigabit. title: Surprise report: New Mac mini could land any day now
content:
Macworld





Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.)
Writing for Bloomberg, well-connected leaker Mark Gurman says Apple is gearing up to unveil the first new Mac mini in almost two years. He bases this on the testimony of unnamed sources “familiar with the matter.”
The last Mac mini model, announced on October 29, 2024, featured a major redesign (it was significantly smaller than its predecessor) as well as a faster M4 chip. This machine has become extremely popular, Gurman says, for running AI applications, but the ongoing memory crunch means Apple has struggled to meet demand. The Mac mini has essentially been out of stock since the spring, with delivery times slipping into months-long waits.
That isn’t to say that Apple necessarily thinks the new model will help in this regard. Gurman acknowledges that it’s unclear “how the new model will affect wait times,” as an updated mini is unlikely to require less memory than the current one. It seems more likely that Apple simply feels it’s time for an update, and the product’s popularity has pushed it to the front of the line.
Gurman’s report is generally short on details, with little information offered regarding design (although we can guess that another redesign would be a surprise so soon after the last one) and tech specs, where he says only that models with both M5 and M6 chips have been tested. The main takeaway regards timings. Gurman says the new Mac mini could arrive ahead of the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, which will appear in early September and likely on September 9, and even says it will likely be the last product to launch under Cook’s watch.
Cook is slated to exit the CEO seat on September 1, which (assuming Gurman’s speculation is correct) gives a window of just seven days for the Mac mini to arrive. And we can rule out most of those days because they’re unsuitable for an announcement; by far the most plausible are Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. It could launch today, in other words.
The mini is only one of the Macs getting an update this fall as part of a massive overhaul. For all the latest news and rumors, bookmark our regularly updated new Mac mini superguide.
creator: Macworld

title: 'MacBook Ultra' Coming Soon With Touchscreen and 5 Other Changes
content:
Reports and rumors suggest the next high-end MacBook Pro that Apple will release might not be a ‌MacBook Pro‌ at all. It could actually be something altogether new and more exciting – a "MacBook Ultra" – marketed as the company's top-tier laptop offering. The device is likely to sit above the current M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros, rather than replace them, suggesting that they will remain on sale.


One thing to state up front is that Apple is expected to stick with the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for its touchscreen "Ultra" model. Apple reportedly plans to skip what would have been the "M6 Pro" and "M6 Max" for more powerful "M7 Pro" and "M7 Max" chips. A new entry-level ‌MacBook Pro‌ with the M6 chip is still expected to launch later this year, while the second-generation MacBook Ultra will adopt M7 chip architecture when it arrives later in 2027.

latest report, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman does not specify a release date for the first MacBook Ultra models, but the wording of his summary of upcoming Macs implies that it could still arrive between October and December this year, barring delays due to the global memory chip shortage.

Below, we've listed the features and changes we are expecting for the MacBook Ultra.

OLED Display

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo say Apple is readying OLED technology for these models, and industry reports corroborate their claims. Samsung Display is said to be making the panels exclusively, and the supplier has invested heavily in an 8.6-generation OLED production line in South Korea. The line reached a key milestone for mass production in May.

OLED presents an overall upgrade over the current mini-LED display technology, bringing deeper colors and a higher contrast ratio with true blacks. In an OLED display, individual pixels turn off instead of dimming when not activated, so there's less light leakage and better power efficiency. OLED displays also tend to have better HDR ouptut than mini-LED, but they don't always match mini-LED brightness levels.

Touchscreen

The new ‌MacBook Pro‌ is expected to become the first Mac to support touch input directly on the display. It's a notable shift from Apple's longstanding position against bringing touchscreen functionality to the Mac. 

Apple previously experimented with touch controls through the OLED Touch Bar on earlier ‌MacBook Pro‌ models, but the feature was ultimately discontinued following a lukewarm reception. Rather than positioning the ‌MacBook Pro‌ as a touch-centric device like the ‌iPad‌, Apple is reportedly planning to let users move seamlessly between touch and traditional trackpad or mouse input across the system.

There are features in ‌macOS Golden Gate‌ that hint at a future touchscreen Mac. Apple added direct touch input to Sidecar so users can tap and interact with macOS elements when using the ‌iPad‌ as a Mac display. macOS Golden Gate‌ also supports an iPhone-style pull-to-refresh option, and it can be used across apps like Safari, Mail, News, Podcasts, and Calendar. A pull-to-refresh option makes the most sense on a touch display.

Reinforced Hinge

Apple has reportedly developed a reinforced hinge and screen hardware to prevent the display from bouncing back or moving when touched. Apple is apparently aware of the same issue that plagues existing touch PCs.

Thinner Design

Gurman has reported that Apple is working to make the OLED MacBook Pro significantly thinner, as part of the company's plan to create "the thinnest and lightest products in their categories across the whole tech industry." (Think the latest iPad Pro and iPad Air – two of the thinnest devices the company has ever made.) Indeed, the reporter has said there's a good chance that the next MacBook Pro model will represent a "true overhaul" for the laptop, thanks to the combination of the OLED display and thinner design.

Notably, the MacBook Pro got thicker and heavier with its most recent redesign in 2021. A major highlight was the reintroduction of several ports that were removed in previous iterations in favor of chassis thinness. How Apple will make its redesigned MacBook Pro thinner without removing the functionality it reintroduced fairly recently is the big question.

Dynamic Island

The MacBook Ultra could ditch the current notch used in the MacBook Pro models for a display cutout potentially similar to the iPhone's Dynamic Island, according to Bloomberg. Such a move would mirror Apple's iPhone evolution, since the iPhone's notch became the current Dynamic Island starting with the iPhone 14 Pro models in 2022. 

As with the iPhone‌, the Mac ‌Dynamic Island‌ will be interactive and it will contextually expand based on the app or Mac feature in use. The change should address long-standing user complaints about the notch, which physically ingresses into the macOS menu bar.

Price Changes

There is no doubt that Apple will unveil the MacBook Ultra as an ultra-premium product carrying a price tag that is higher than the current MacBook Pro 14-inch and 16-inch models. Apple increased the prices of all its Macs in June 2026 – MacBook Pro‌ pricing went up $300 – so the MacBook Ultra will likely be even more expensive than expected. ‌

title: iPhone Trade-In Values Slide Ahead of New Model Launch
content:
Ahead of the announcement of the iPhone 18 Pro, ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max, and first foldable iPhone next month, a new study from trade-in comparison site SellCell finds that most iPhones lose a considerable amount of trade-in value in the 10-day window between Apple's announcement and the actual product launch.


Looking at the launch of the iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 lineups, SellCell found that trade-in values dropped for 117 of 156 models tracked, or 75% of the total, between announcement day and release day. That window saw the steepest declines for the ‌iPhone 17‌ lineup last year, with 50 of 54 iPhone models (92.6%) losing value, with an average drop of $36.46 per device.

The largest individual declines came from older models still on the trade-in market at the time. The ‌iPhone 16‌ Plus 512GB fell from $695 to $566, a $129 drop and the largest loss in the dataset. The iPhone 15 Plus 128GB saw the steepest percentage decline, falling from $440 to $351, a loss of 20.2%.

SellCell paired the pricing data with a survey of 2,000 U.S. iPhone users. 61.4% of respondents said they plan to keep their current iPhone until a replacement is in hand and set up, rather than trading it in around the announcement. The most common reasons cited were needing the phone for continued use and needing to transfer data, which together accounted for 77.4% of responses.

updated and largely increased its own official trade-in estimates last month ahead of the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and foldable iPhone announcement.

title: 20th Anniversary iPhone: Everything we know so far
content:
Macworld





The original iPhone was released on June 29, 2007. So next year, it will turn 20 years old, and rumors point to Apple commemorating the event with a special 20th-anniversary model.
It’s not expected to launch on June 29 (it will probably be in September, as usual), and it may not be a special one-off product, but rather the next major evolution of the iPhone, much like the iPhone X in 2017. But either way, the big two-oh is supposed to bring something really special.
Here’s what we’ve gleaned from the rumors and leaks so far.
20th Anniversary iPhone: What to expect
Major redesign: Apple is expected to mark the iPhone’s 20th anniversary in 2027 with a near-all-screen design, curved glass, ultra-thin bezels, and two Pro-sized models.
Display upgrades: Face ID could move under the display, leaving only a small punch-hole front camera for a cleaner look.
Key hardware improvements: Rumored upgrades include a new Sony camera sensor, solid-state haptic buttons, and a silicon-anode battery for better battery life.
More powerful internals: The phone is expected to feature the A21 Pro chip, C3 modem, and improved wireless connectivity for better performance and efficiency.
Premium positioning: Expected to launch in September 2027, with a starting price of around $1,299 or more.


What will the 20th Anniversary iPhone be called?
iPhone XX is a possible name
iPhone 19 could arrive alongside the special edition 

				
					

				
			
Steve Jobs demonstrating  the first iPhone in January 2007.

Apple




They say history doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme. We may be looking at that sort of thing in 2027.
In 2017, for the iPhone’s tenth anniversary, Apple skipped over the “iPhone 9” entirely and introduced the iPhone X, which brought with it a set of new design elements and technologies that would go on to define the iPhone for the next decade: a full OLED display with no Home button, Face ID, and wireless charging. It also cost more than any iPhone had before, starting at $999.
For the 20th anniversary, Apple may simply call it iPhone 20. It should be noted that we might also get an iPhone 19 at the same event, just as Apple introduced the iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus at the same event as the iPhone X. Since we’re getting an iPhone 18 this year, iPhone 19 might join iPhone 20 (or maybe iPhone XX, as some media outlets have dubbed it) as a cheaper option next year.


						

							


When will the 20th Anniversary iPhone launch?
Likely release date: September 2027
There has been no hard information on the 20th Anniversary iPhone’s release date yet, but it is generally expected to launch in the typical time frame for iPhones: an announcement in September and an on-sale in late September or October 2027.
An August 2026 report from a financial analyst at Jefferies claimed that Apple has scrapped the 20th Anniversary iPhone entirely over costs. We haven’t heard this from other sources yet, and it was quickly debunked by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Financial analysts don’t always have the best track record of leaking future Apple product plans, but it’s worth noting.


						

							


How much will the 20th Anniversary iPhone cost?
High starting price of $1,299 or more
It’s too early to predict what the RAM crunch will do to next year’s prices, but we expect the 20th Anniversary iPhone to be expensive. With more advanced technology than most “Pro” iPhones, the starting price will likely be at least $1,299, if not more.


						

							


What will the 20th Anniversary iPhone look like?
Two sizes similar to the current Pro hones
Edge-to-edge displays
Curved glass design
One of the defining visual characteristics of the 20th Anniversary iPhone will reportedly be its all-display look. Leaks have described the handset as having “a quad-curved screen design,” with the idea being that the phone will appear to be one big display. Bezels could be minimized to the point where you don’t even see them, and the glass will curve down on all four sides. It’s been reported that Apple could adopt its Liquid Glass branding as well.
Reports suggest that Apple is preparing two models, roughly equivalent to the current Pro and Pro Max iPhones at around 6.3 and 6.9 inches, which would be the largest iPhone Apple has ever made.


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have a Dynamic Island?
Under-display Face ID expected
Hole-punch camera for selfie cam rumored

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




One of the persistent rumors over the past several years is that Apple will continue to put more front camera system components under the display, until it’s all display with no cutouts at all.
That may be several years away, but at least some of the components might be able to go behind the OLED display. One rumor claims that Apple will use a “spliced micro-transparent glass,” which will allow it to put the IR emitter under the display, leaving just the regular camera and maybe the IR receiving camera in a cutout region. If the IR camera can effectively go under the display as well, the 20th Anniversary iPhone will have just a single round punch-hole camera in front but retain Face ID.


						

							


What camera will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have?
Customize LOFIC image sensor
Triple-camera array with telephoto lens
200MP camera possible

				
					

				
			
Stephan Wiesend




According to a Korean-language blog post by a leaker who goes by yeux1122 (who has been accurate in the past with some supply-chain scoops), Apple is working together with Sony on a custom image sensor that uses LOFIC (Lateral Integral Overflow Capacitor) technology.
Phone makers Honor, Xiaomi, and Huawei all use sensors with LOFIC technology in their flagship phones now. It’s a technique that allows sensors to capture low-light or dark areas of an image with less noise, along with brighter areas of an image, without increasing ISO sensitivity. In other words, it gives the camera more dynamic range with less noise.
Otherwise, we expect the 20th Anniversary iPhone to have a triple-camera system like the current Pro models, with wide, ultrawide, and telephoto cameras. It’s likely that the cameras will have significant upgrades, however, with a possible 200MP lens.


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have physical buttons?
Current buttons will reportedly remain
Solid-state with haptics could replace physical buttons

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




On all current MacBooks (other than MacBook Neo), the trackpad doesn’t actually move. Instead, it produces the sensation of being clicked using precise haptic feedback. It’s very effective and reduces the possibility of breakage due to fewer moving parts.
The 20th Anniversary iPhone is supposed to replace the power, volume, Action, and Camera Control buttons with parts that operate in a similar way. These buttons wouldn’t move at all. Rather, they will be integrated into the frame itself, but will have touch capacitors and haptics to give them the feel of a actual button.
Weibo account Instant Digital (with a mixed track record) says extensive testing is ongoing to make sure these new solid-state haptic buttons work well with gloves, cases, wet hands, and so on. 
If Apple can pull this off and they feel as good as real buttons, it will be an important part of the durability of the new iPhone. With the display glass curving down on all edges, the edge area of the frame itself will be very thin, and further cutouts to accommodate buttons would make it less likey to resist bending.


						

							


What specs will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have?
New Apple chips—A21, C3, and more
12GB or 16GB of RAM
We’ve got the A20 Pro processor coming in this year’s iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra. Next year we expect the A21, using a refined 2nm manufacturing process and further improving performance.
Apple’s C-series modems are on a roughly yearly cadence, or so it is claimed. We should see the C2 this year, but it may not be used in the flagship iPhones in the U.S. Next year, it is said, the C3 will be ready for release, and could appear in every iPhone, globally. Each successive C-series modem should improve wireless speed and reliability while improving battery life.
Apple has another networking chip, the N1, which provides Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 capabilities. It’s already in a few products and should show up in the 2026 iPhones as well. Will Apple be ready with an N2 in time for the 20th Anniversary iPhone? It wouldn’t be strictly necessary from a features perspective, but an updated chip might improve wireless performance while reducing power use.
Based on what we expect from the iPhone 18 Pro, we assume the 20th Anniversary iPhone will have at least 12GB of RAM and possibly as much as 16GB, depending on what AI capabilities Apple builds into it. 


						

							


Will the 20th Anniversary iPhone have longer battery life?
New battery technology
A report from ETNews in 2025 said that Apple is looking to use a battery with a pure silicon anode in the 20th Anniversary iPhone.
This change in battery chemistry increases energy density, so you can pack more charge into a smaller volume. Both the OnePlus 15 and the Oppo Find X9 Pro use this battery technology today to deliver batteries with a capacity around 7,300 mAh. That’s about 40% more capacity than you’ll find in an iPhone 17 Pro Max.

title: It’s Tim Cook’s last week on the job. Let’s review his career
content:
Macworld





Congrats to Tim Cook on his 15-year anniversary as CEO of Apple! Here are some balloons and a gift card to the Olive Garden. There will be cake in the break room.
It occurs to this furry observer that this is his last column before Tim Cook steps down as CEO of Apple. Hard to believe. The sad truth is that pretty soon we won’t have Tim Cook to kick around anymore. Other than the fact that he will still be working for the company, just in a different capacity, and we will absolutely still have him to kick around.
Still, it’s worth reviewing Cook’s tenure as Apple CEO. Apple loves it when you write reviews, right? So let’s get into it!
The Macalope’s not going to focus on politics. Apparently, there are some people who do not like it when the Macalope discusses politics. That wouldn’t stop the horny one in any way from talking about it (it might even encourage him), but he thinks he’s already been clear about his feelings on Cook’s recent forays into the political world and Cook hasn’t done anything of late to really get the antlers itching, if you know what the Macalope means (you don’t and you do not want to). The Macalope has no idea what Cook’s personal politics are. He suspects they probably pretty much align with his own. Cook’s business politics, however, would best be driven out to a rural town and gently tipped into an underground coal fire, never to be seen again.
So, it’s a little rich (allusion intended) when the Macalope sees things like this:
I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I feel like I have achieved something.
Apple CEO Tim Cook (CBS News interview, August 13, 2026)
Mmm. Sorry, Tim. You might need a time machine for that.
But let’s just look at Cook’s legacy as a simple CEO running a small business in downtown Cupertino.
If you’re an Apple investor, it’s hard not to think of Cook as one of the greatest CEOs of all time. The Macalope’s not going to bother to look it up and figure it out with stock splits and buybacks and all the free coffee distributed and t-shirts shot out of a canon at shareholders meetings, but if you invested 15 years ago when Cook took over, you have to be happy with the returns.
(Hilariously, 15 years ago is about exactly when the Macalope sold the two (2) shares of Apple stock he owned.)
As someone who regularly had to deal with nincompoops who continued to say Apple was going to go out of business long after it made a lick of sense, the Macalope owes Cook a personal debt of gratitude for finally making it clear that that was not a thing you could say anymore and be taken seriously by anyone.
Despite the insistence of many that Apple hasn’t released any truly great products since Steve Jobs died, Apple has actually released some truly great products since Steve Jobs died. Sure, none of them have been as world-changing as the iPhone, the greatest consumer electronics product of all time, but, you know, that’s a pretty high bar. The Apple Watch, loudly declared a flop for years, is everywhere, as are AirPods, and Apple TV continues to churn out hit shows and movies.

				
					

				
			
If you’d like to receive regular news and updates to your inbox, sign up for our newsletters, including The Macalope and Apple Breakfast, David Price’s weekly, bite-sized roundup of all the latest Apple news and rumors.

Foundry




Other products, such as the Vision Pro, have not fared as well: Apple lays off 200 employees to focus on ‘new devices’ and AI.
Overall, however, the story of Apple’s growth in the last 15 years is astounding and Cook is largely the architect of that growth.
This is not to say everything has been hunky-dory. Honestly, who even says “hunky-dory” anymore? At all? How many of today’s youths have even heard the phrase?
All these old-timey aphorisms will be lost in time… like tears in the rain…
W-what was the Macalope saying? Oh, right, the bad stuff.
Apple’s relationship with developers can best be described by riffing on the old saw about Britain and the U.S. and describing it as “two business partners, separated by an app store”. This, however, seems like one of those areas where Jobs, who didn’t even want to have an app store in the first place, would have largely done exactly the same thing.
Like with developers, Cook has consistently made sure that Apple comes out on top in its relationship with customers as well. Everything is a subscription now. Used to be you could tie an onion to your belt and buy some gub-danged software. Not anymore. Apple gets revenue that’s as smooth as ice, and we get tithed more and more every year.
Indeed, Cook has not even been afraid to degrade Apple’s vaunted user experience in order to make a buck. Ads for junk apps not remotely related to what you’re interested in pop up over search results in the App Store; Apple News will show you AI-generated ad for products that don’t even exist, and–yay!–ads are coming to Maps! (Disclaimer: not “Yay!”) Again, if you’re an Apple investor, the services revenue generated by all this is great. If you’re a customer, it sucks.
If you want to judge Tim Cook as a businessman, well, he’s tops; there’s no denying it. In fact, he might just be a little too good. But if Cook really wanted to be remembered as “good” and “decent,” well, he might have read the notes we were giving him all along the way.
Three stars. Should be cheaper.

title: Best Thunderbolt and USB-C docking stations for your MacBook 2026
content:
Macworld





Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.  
Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C
The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.
USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps
USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps
Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps
Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps
Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.
While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.
The dock needs one (“upstream“) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“downstream“) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.
For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.
Add external displays to your MacBook
If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk. Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.
You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI). Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac. DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.
More explained: we cover more on Mac docking stations and external displays at the end of this feature below our recommendations.
Do I need a docking station?
With three TB4 or TB5 and an HDMI port, a MacBook with a Max chip could connect to up to four external displays without the need for a dock, although such a power user would likely require extra Thunderbolt and other ports for more devices to make up for using all the laptop ports for multiple monitors. See below our list of recommended docking stations for more detail on the external display options with each recent MacBook.
All docks come with a bunch of USB ports: some old-school USB-A and newer, more capable USB-C. MacBook Pros also have an SD card reader. Although this card reader is rated as UHS-II (312MBps), Apple has pegged it back at 250MBps, so for the fastest speeds (and a microSD slot if you need one), a dock will likely be a better choice for memory-card use if it is rated at UHS-II rather than UHS-I (104MBps).
MacBooks also lack wired Internet access via an Ethernet port, so if you want to escape flaky Wi-Fi, buy a dock with at least Gigabit Ethernet, although you could add a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter instead if you have a spare TB port. Some later docks include faster 2.5Gb, 5Gb or even 10Gb Ethernet but you’ll need a supporting router or other device to get the benefits, although these faster Ethernet ports are backwards compatible with Gigabit so will future-proof your purchase.
Dock or hub?
If you need just a few extra ports, a USB-C hub or Thunderbolt hub might be your best choice—see our roundup of the best USB-C and Thunderbolt hubs for Mac. However, if you require a bunch of fast ports including Gigabit (or faster) Ethernet and multiple video ports plus more powerful charging capability, then look for a full dock that fulfils your needs. We’ve reviewed the best hubs alongside the docks.

USB PD: Power Delivery for your laptop
Most docks can charge the connected MacBook, so look for the right Power Delivery (PD) rating that suits your laptop. You can’t over-power a MacBook so the simplest advice is to aim as high as you can. 70W will be more than enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air but go for 85W or more (PD 3.0) for a MacBook Pro, and 140W (PD 3.1) for the top-end 16-inch Pro.

Which ports are on each MacBook?
Of Apple’s recent laptop ranges, the M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air and 14-inch M3 MacBook Pro feature two ports that Apple specified as “Thunderbolt / USB 4” ports, while more recent the 13in and 15in M4/M5 MacBook Air models feature two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The 14in and 16in M1/M2/M3 Pro, plain M4/M5 MacBook Pro, and M1/M2/M3 Max MacBook Pro models come with three Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) ports. Ignore Apple’s dual designation of non-4 Thunderbolt and USB4—it just means that the ports don’t certify as pure Thunderbolt 4, and that shouldn’t worry most users except for the number of external displays each supports.
Apple’s latest M4/M5 Pro and M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro models feature three of the latest Thunderbolt 5 ports, which are backwards compatible with TB4, TB3 and USB-C. They promise 80Gbps data transfer and 120Gbps video rates. Until the technology finds its way into more devices and the Thunderbolt 5 dock market matures, you are still going to do very well with a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 dock, but Thunderbolt 5 docks are fast becoming the norm for new releases.
Thunderbolt 5 frees the latest top-end M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBooks from the two-display limitation forced on them by the macOS’s lack of MST (Multi Stream Transport) support. The M5 Pro now supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt connection and the M5 Max up to four. To reach four external displays most docks reviewed here would need to daisy-chain the fourth display off one of the others.
The entry-level MacBook Neo utilizes lower-spec USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, with 10Gbps rather than Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps or 80Gbps. A USB-C dock is therefore all you should need but it will work with Thunderbolt, which is backwards compatible, but limited to the Neo’s 10Gbps bandwidth.

				
					

				
			The latest MacBook Pro models boast three Thunderbolt 5 ports.
Apple




MacBook built-in ports listed
MacBook Neo: Two USB-C ports, plus headphone jack. One USB-C port is charging only; the other supports video and data up to 10Gbps as well as charging.
13-inch and 15-inch M1/M2/M3 MacBook Air: Two Thunderbolt/USB4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack
13-inch and 15-inch M4/M5 MacBook Air: Two Thunderbolt 4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack
13-inch M1/M2 MacBook Pro: Two Thunderbolt/USB4 ports and one MagSafe 3 charging port, plus headphone jack
14-inch M3 MacBook Pro: Two Thunderbolt/USB4 ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
14-inch M1/M2/M3 Pro, M1/M2/M3 Max and plain M4/M5 MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
14-inch M4/M5 Pro or M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
16-inch M1/M2/M3 Pro or M1/M2/M3 Max MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
16-inch M4/M5 Pro or M4/M5 Max MacBook Pro: Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, one HDMI port, one SDXC card slot, plus headphone jack
How many external displays can each MacBook support without a dock?
Neo: One external display with up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. Use a DisplayLink dock for more than one monitor on the MacBook Neo.
M1/M2: One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz. Use a DisplayLink dock for more than one monitor on these MacBooks.
M3: Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 5K/60Hz when the MacBook lid is closed.
M4: Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 5K/60Hz.
M5: Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port, one with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz and one at 6K/60Hz.
M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro: Up to two external displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt, or one external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display at 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
M1/M2/M3/M4 Max: Up to four external displays: Up to three external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 4K resolution at 144Hz over HDMI. Up to three external displays: Up to two external displays with 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one external display with up to 8K resolution at 60Hz or one external display with 4K resolution at 240Hz over HDMI.
M5 Pro: Supports up to three external displays over a single Thunderbolt port. Up to three displays up to a native resolution of 6K (6144 x 3456) at 60Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 144Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI. Or one external display supported at 8K (7680 x 4320) at 60Hz, 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz, or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 240Hz, plus a second display up to a native resolution of 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 200Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI.
M5 Max: Supports up to four external displays over a single Thunderbolt port. Up to four displays up to a native resolution of 6K (6144 x 3456) at 60Hz or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 144Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI. Two displays up to a native resolution of 8K (7680 x 4320) at 60Hz, 5K (5120 x 2880) at 120Hz, or 4K (3840 x 2160) at 240Hz over Thunderbolt or HDMI.
Mac docking stations and external displays

				
					

				
			
Baseus




While Apple’s MacBooks featuring the company’s own M-series Silicon chips are super speedy compared to the models sporting Intel processors, models with plain (non-Pro or -Max) M1 and M2 chips come with an incredible limitation: they don’t support more than one external display in Extended Mode even via their Thunderbolt ports. Plain M3 MacBooks can support two displays but only with their lids closed. The MacBook Neo uses a different A18 Pro chip and has the same single-monitor limitation as the plain M1 and M2.
This limitation means that when using any docking station, M1/M2 and Neo MacBook users cannot extend their desktop over two or more displays, and will be limited to either dual Mirrored displays or one external display—although adding third-party DisplayLink or InstantView software to the Mac and connecting to a dedicated USB-C dock will allow you to add more than one external monitor to an M1, M2 or M3 MacBook. Follow that link for our roundup of the best USB-C DisplayLink docks, and we’ve included our favorite in our roundup above.
In the example above, standard M1/M2/Neo Macs would require DisplayLink to achieve Extended Mode 2. M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max and standard M3/M4/M5 onwards can natively work in that mode without DisplayLink but would require it for three or more extended screens. M5 Pro supports three screens, and M5 Max supports four, without requiring DisplayLink.
Above, we’ve listed the native external display options for each MacBook. Thunderbolt 5 docks should support up to four 6K displays if you own an M5 Max-chip MacBook Pro.
While some docking stations promise support for 8K displays, Macs are limited to 6K support via the dock. Macs with an M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip can support an 8K display at 60Hz but only when it is connected via the Mac’s own HDMI port and not any port on the dock.
Dock, hub or dongle: Whole lotta ports
You need one (“upstream“) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although the 14/16in MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe port), and likely at least another (“downstream“) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).
There are many inexpensive USB-C dongles/hubs that let you add more devices to a MacBook (see our roundup of the best USB-C adapters for Macs) or a Thunderbolt hub offering a few extra ports might be all your need, but for maximum flexibility check out a docking station that takes care of all your extra port requirements, and allows you to simply attach it to your laptop with just one cable when you get to the office or come home.
Docks aren’t just for MacBooks. Mac mini (2018 and later) and iMac (2017 and later) owners may also consider expanding their ports with a Thunderbolt docking station.
The inclusion of an SD or microSD card reader isn’t just for camera buffs. It’s a convenient and affordable way to add storage to your laptop setup. We found a 512GB Samsung Evo microSD card on Amazon for around $100 in the US and under £100 in the UK. That’s a very cheap way of adding half a terabyte of portable storage. For more details read up on our best microSD cards.
Some of the docks reviewed above include an integrated SSD enclosure that lets you add up to 8TB of fast storage to your connected MacBook.
Charging the laptop
While the MacBook Neo can get by on 20W Power Delivery (PD), the M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 MacBook Air requires a PD charger with at least 30W power, but you can fast-charge an M2 and later Air with a charger rated at over 70W. You’ll need 67W for the 13-inch MacBook Pro and 70W for the 14-inch MBP (with 8-, 10-, 11-or 12-core CPU), 96W for 14-inch MBP (with 12- or 14-core CPU), and 96W (preferably 140W) for the 16-inch MBP. The older 15in MacBook Pro requires a 87W PD charger.
If you own a larger MacBook Pro, buy a dock with a PD (Power Delivery) potential of at least 85W if you can. USB PD 3.0 maxes at 100W, while USB PD 3.1 can support up to 240W of power. The 16-inch MacBook Pro requires 140W to fast-charge, so owners of that laptop should look for a PD 3.1 charger.
If you just need a spare charger, we’ve tested the best MacBook chargers for you.
Other dock options
Here we concentrate on Thunderbolt docks, but also include cheaper USB-C docks—which Thunderbolt MacBooks can use, but at the cost of reduced bandwidth and display limitations. We’ve also included our favorite Thunderbolt hubs for smaller and cheaper alternatives. For more non-Thunderbolt USB-C-only docks check out Tech Advisor’s roundup of the best USB-C docking stations for laptops. Tech Advisor also reviews all the available Thunderbolt 4 docks.
Now think about a stand to go alongside the dock
These MacBook docking stations look and work great with a laptop stand, and we’ve also tested some MacBook-friendly stands that lack all the extra ports but keep your MacBook/Air/Pro upright and out of the way: further saving valuable desk space, reducing clutter, keeping your laptop cool, and saving it from spills.

title: Handy disk image tool is getting removed from macOS
content:
In future releases of macOS, Mac users will no longer be able to format or eject disk images using the very long-standing Terminal command, hdiutil. It won't affect many users directly, but it could well break disk repair utility apps.


The new deprecation notice in Terminal for the command hdiutil.
You may never have even heard of it, but since the earliest days of Mac OS X, the Terminal has included the command now called hdiutil. It's a tool for handling disk images, and AppleInsider forum users have often recommended it for solving problems such as the Mac refusing to eject such disk images because they're purportedly in use.
As first spotted by developer Jeff Johnson, however, Apple is officially deprecating hdultil in macOS Golden Gate. What this means is that you, and app utilities, can continue using it for now, but should switch to the similar diskutil image command as ultimately hdiutil will be removed.

unify the email domains used by Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email under a single private.icloud.com domain. iPhone users expressed concern that moving Hide My Email to a private.icloud.com domain instead of icloud.com would let platforms easily block iCloud aliases. title: iOS 27 beta 7 is out now as the general release date approaches
content:
Macworld





On the first day of the WWDC developer conference, Apple released the first developer beta of its new operating system. This year, that means that the first release of iOS 27 outside Cupertino came on June 8, 2026.
The pattern goes like this: Apple releases developer-only betas for the first month or so, and then starts releasing the same build for both developers and public beta testers. With only a month or less before the general release, most of the beta updates now are minor in scope, focused on polish, optimization, and fixing the last bugs.
If you want to try out the new OS 27 updates and provide feedback, check out our article on how to become a beta tester. It’s easy.
Updated August 24, 2026: The seventh beta of iOS 27 is now available to developers, and should be released to the public testers within the next day or so.
What’s new in iOS 27
The big iOS 27 release this year is focused on three main areas:
Trust and Safety – New parental controls to keep kids safe and control screen time.
Performance and refinement – Speeding everything up, improving efficiency, tweaking interfaces, and addressing dozens of small user requests.
Apple Intelligence and Siri – Entirely new Apple Intelligence models improve AI throughout the system, and a brand-new Siri is vastly more capable than ever before.
For a more complete breakdown of all the new features and changes, check out our iOS 27 guide.
Beta 6 primarily fine-tuned some animations and interface behaviors while optimizing performance. We expect Beta 7 to have similar small refinements, as the general release is getting really close now.
iOS 27: How to install the developer beta
You’ll need to be registered as an Apple Developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:
Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
Open the app.
Tap on Account.
Sign in using your usual Apple ID.
Once you have a free developer account, just follow the same instructions as with the public beta:
Open Settings.
Tap General, then Software Update.
Make sure the Beta Updates selection is set to iOS 27 Developer Beta.
Follow the on-screen instructions.
iOS 27: How to install the public beta
The first iOS 27 public beta is not available yet but is expected to arrive in July. When it lands, you can follow these steps to test it out even if you’re not a developer:
Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
Log in to the Beta Software Program.
Click Enroll your iOS device.
Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS 27 Public Beta.
It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update. 
If you want to uninstall the iOS 27 beta read: How to remove an iOS beta from your iPhone.

title: Apple Holds Farewell Party for Tim Cook as Ternus Prepares to Take Over
content:
Tim Cook will step down as Apple's CEO on Tuesday, September 1, and ahead of that date, Apple hosted a farewell party for him. According to The Information, the party took place on August 23, just a day before Cook celebrated his 15th anniversary as Apple CEO.


Approximately 200 people celebrated Cook at the Caffé Macs cafeteria on the Apple campus, and band OneRepublic performed. Several speakers shared tributes to Cook, including Steve Jobs' wife Laurene Powell Jobs, former Apple COO Jeff Williams, Apple services chief Eddy Cue, and incoming CEO John Ternus.


.@OneRepublic at Apple Park Cupertino HQ with outgoing Apple CEO @tim_cook 
📷 Brody Harper pic.twitter.com/LSqtAidmBJ
— OneRepublic News (@1RNews) August 24, 2026
 

Cook is not leaving Apple, despite the party. Next Tuesday, he will become Apple's executive chairman, where he will "assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world." Cook will spend less time in the spotlight in his new role.

Ternus has been at Apple since 2001, serving as senior vice president of hardware engineering since 2021. Apple's September iPhone event will be his first major product launch as CEO.

The Information that continuity is the focus of the transition from Cook to Ternus, with few things to change. Cook's executive assistant will stay on and work for Ternus.
